A three-arm trial: deficit and dependence

Source: vignettes/three-arm-trial.Rmd
three-arm-trial.Rmd
library(pollinatoR)

The design

A three-arm trial puts three pollination treatments side by side: plants excluded from insects (caged or bagged), plants left open to whatever pollinators visit, and plants supplemented by hand with extra pollen. The three arms answer two different questions.

  • The deficit (E1) compares supplemented with open plants. It asks how much yield was left on the table by the pollination the crop actually received.
  • The dependence (E2) compares excluded plants with a reference arm. It asks how much yield is owed to pollinators. The reference is usually the open arm; in a three-arm trial it can also be the supplemented arm, which gives the dependence under full pollination.

This vignette simulates a small randomised complete block trial: eight blocks, each holding all three arms, with six plants per arm in each block. The response is pod count per plant.

set.seed(2024)
n_block <- 8L
n_plant <- 6L
arms <- c("Bagged", "Open", "Hand")
trial <- expand.grid(
  plant = seq_len(n_plant),
  trt = arms,
  block = sprintf("B%d", seq_len(n_block)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
block_effect <- rnorm(n_block, 0, 0.15)
arm_mean <- c(Bagged = 40, Open = 60, Hand = 70)
names(block_effect) <- sprintf("B%d", seq_len(n_block))
mu <- arm_mean[trial$trt] * exp(block_effect[trial$block])
trial$pods <- rnbinom(nrow(trial), mu = mu, size = 30)
head(trial)
#>   plant    trt block pods
#> 1     1 Bagged    B1   32
#> 2     2 Bagged    B1   55
#> 3     3 Bagged    B1   54
#> 4     4 Bagged    B1   66
#> 5     5 Bagged    B1   65
#> 6     6 Bagged    B1   55

The planted arm means are 40, 60 and 70 pods. On these values the dependence on the open arm is a loss share of 1−40/60=0.331 - 40/60 = 0.33, and the deficit is a loss share of 1−60/70=0.141 - 60/70 = 0.14.

Data, design and estimand

The data step names the columns; the design step maps each treatment level to its role and fixes the layout. In a randomised complete block layout the block carries a random intercept.

pd <- pollin_data(trial, response = "pods", treatment = "trt", unit = "block")
ds <- pollin_design(
  pd,
  arms = c(excluded = "Bagged", open = "Open", supplemented = "Hand"),
  layout = "rcbd"
)
ds
#> <pollin_design>
#>   layout    : rcbd 
#>   arms      : excluded = Bagged, open = Open, supplemented = Hand 
#>   reference : open 
#>   units     : block 
#>   random    : (1 | block)

The estimand step names the contrast, the scale and the basis. Neither the scale nor the basis has a default.

deficit <- pollin_estimand(ds, family = "deficit", scale = "ratio", basis = "loss")
deficit
#> <pollin_estimand>
#>   family     : deficit (E1) 
#>   contrast   : Hand vs Open 
#>   scale      : ratio 
#>   basis      : loss 
#>   population : trial 
#>   layout     : rcbd 
#>   assumptions: 6 ; see `pollin_assumptions()`
knitr::kable(pollin_assumptions(deficit))
assumption statement
consistency Each arm is one well-defined treatment, applied the same way on every unit.
excludability Hand supplementation changes the response only through the pollen added (no damage from handling).
no_interference One unit’s treatment does not change another unit’s response, for example by displacing pollinators to neighbouring units.
assignment Arms were randomised to units within each block.
positive_means The expected response is positive in both arms, so the ratio is defined.
population The estimand refers to the units in the trial; carrying it to other fields or seasons is a further assumption.

The assumption table is the part of the analysis the data cannot check. For the deficit, the key one is that hand supplementation adds pollen and nothing else; for the dependence, it is that the bag or cage excludes insects without changing the plant’s microclimate.

Loss share or gain

The same pair of arm means can be reported in two ways. The loss share is the fraction of the higher arm’s yield that is lost without the contrast, 1−low/high1 - \mathrm{low}/\mathrm{high}. The gain is the increase over the lower arm, high/low−1\mathrm{high}/\mathrm{low} - 1. For the dependence planted here, the loss share is 0.33 and the gain is 0.50. The two answer different questions: the loss share is the part of current yield that pollinators supply, which is what a valuation of their service needs, and the gain is how much a crop without them would rise if they returned. Reporting a gain where a loss share was meant overstates the value by a factor of 1/(1−D)1/(1 - D).

basis is therefore stated every time, and printed on every result.

fit_effect <- function(design, family, scale, basis) {
  est <- pollin_estimand(design, family = family, scale = scale, basis = basis)
  pollin_effects(pollin_fit(est))$table
}
dep_loss <- fit_effect(ds, "dependence", "ratio", "loss")
dep_gain <- fit_effect(ds, "dependence", "ratio", "gain")
rbind(dep_loss, dep_gain)[, c("contrast", "basis", "estimate", "conf.low", "conf.high")]
#>         contrast basis  estimate  conf.low conf.high
#> 1 Open vs Bagged  loss 0.3059873 0.2411880 0.3652530
#> 2 Open vs Bagged  gain 0.4408958 0.3178495 0.5754309

The interval for a ratio-type scale is a delta interval for the log ratio of the averaged predictions, transformed to the scale, so a loss share stays below one.

Both intervals cover the planted values. A parametric bootstrap gives a second interval: responses are simulated from the fitted model, the model is refitted to each simulated set, and the interval is taken from the percentiles of the refitted estimates. Use several hundred refits in an analysis; the 100 here keep the example quick.

est_dep <- pollin_estimand(ds, family = "dependence", scale = "ratio", basis = "loss")
pollin_effects(pollin_fit(est_dep), interval = "bootstrap", n_boot = 100L, seed = 1L)
#> <pollin_effects>
#>   family   : dependence (E2) 
#>   scale    : ratio 
#>   basis    : loss 
#>   estimate : 1 - Bagged/Open (loss share) 
#>   interval : 95% parametric bootstrap (100 refits) 
#>  response       contrast  estimate  std.error  conf.low conf.high p.value
#>      pods Open vs Bagged 0.3059873 0.03188554 0.2424225 0.3655036      NA
#>      family scale basis distribution  interval
#>  dependence ratio  loss      nbinom2 bootstrap

Both estimands on several scales

The estimate is always formed from the model’s expected response in each arm, averaged over the trial’s plants: a ratio of averaged predictions, never an average of plant-level ratios. The scale only changes how that pair of expected values is reported.

grid <- expand.grid(
  family = c("deficit", "dependence"),
  scale = c("difference", "ratio", "rii", "lnrr"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
rows <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(grid)), function(i) {
  fit_effect(ds, grid$family[i], grid$scale[i], basis = "loss")
})
effects <- do.call(rbind, rows)
effects[, c("family", "contrast", "scale", "estimate", "conf.low", "conf.high")]
#>       family       contrast      scale    estimate    conf.low  conf.high
#> 1    deficit   Hand vs Open difference  8.81219559  2.83154691 14.7928443
#> 2 dependence Open vs Bagged difference 19.94446792 14.75439295 25.1345429
#> 3    deficit   Hand vs Open      ratio  0.11909515  0.04065030  0.1911257
#> 4 dependence Open vs Bagged      ratio  0.30598730  0.24118799  0.3652530
#> 5    deficit   Hand vs Open        rii  0.06331801  0.02074683  0.1056600
#> 6 dependence Open vs Bagged        rii  0.18062869  0.13713119  0.2234309
#> 7    deficit   Hand vs Open       lnrr  0.12680566  0.04149962  0.2121117
#> 8 dependence Open vs Bagged       lnrr  0.36526501  0.27600121  0.4545288

The RII and the loss share are linked by RII=D/(2−D)\mathrm{RII} = D/(2 - D), and the log response ratio is log⁡(high/low)\log(\mathrm{high}/\mathrm{low}), so the three ratio-type rows for each family carry the same information on different scales. All rows here use basis = "loss"; the basis changes the value only on the ratio scale. The difference scale is in pods per plant.

Dependence against the supplemented arm

With reference = "supplemented" the dependence compares excluded plants with hand-pollinated ones. This is the dependence under full pollination, an upper reference for the crop’s need for pollinators, while the open reference gives the dependence realised in the field.

ds_sup <- pollin_design(
  pd,
  arms = c(excluded = "Bagged", open = "Open", supplemented = "Hand"),
  layout = "rcbd",
  reference = "supplemented"
)
est_sup <- pollin_estimand(ds_sup, "dependence", scale = "ratio", basis = "loss")
pollin_effects(pollin_fit(est_sup))
#> <pollin_effects>
#>   family   : dependence (E2) 
#>   scale    : ratio 
#>   basis    : loss 
#>   estimate : 1 - Bagged/Hand (loss share) 
#>   interval : 95% delta 
#>   note     : delta intervals cover fixed-effect uncertainty only
#>  response       contrast  estimate  std.error  conf.low conf.high      p.value
#>      pods Hand vs Bagged 0.3886408 0.02758782 0.3321065 0.4403898 1.096722e-27
#>      family scale basis distribution interval
#>  dependence ratio  loss      nbinom2    delta

A guard on plant-level ratios

A common shortcut computes the RII or the dependence ratio for each block (or each plant) and averages them. The mean of bounded unit-level ratios is not the ratio of the expected values, and pollin_guard_bounded() refuses it unless asked.

try(pollin_guard_bounded(ds, index = "dependence"))
#> Error : Averaging bounded per-unit ratios is not the ratio of expected values; the mean of 8 unit-level dependence values is not the trial's dependence. The dependence of the arm means is 0.3075. Set `allow = TRUE` to average them anyway.

When the average is wanted for comparison with earlier work, allow = TRUE returns it with the statement attached and the ratio of the arm means beside it.

pollin_guard_bounded(ds, index = "dependence", allow = TRUE)
#> <pollin_bounded>  average of unit-level dependence values
#>   mean of 8 units : 0.3004
#>   dependence of arm means : 0.3075
#>   Averaging bounded per-unit ratios is not the ratio of expected values; the mean of 8 unit-level dependence values is not the trial's dependence.

Here the block means differ only a little, so the two numbers are close. They separate when units differ widely in yield, which is common across sites and varieties.
